matrix-multiplication.openai-matrix-nine-fourths-2026: OpenAI's paper describes matrix multiplication by a tensor, a three-way array of numbers, and bounds it with explicit reductions between tensors together with numerical invariants that compare them. It derives inequalities for multiplying polynomials, then uses how those values grow to bound matrix multiplication. The key step separates blocks that already use independent variables in two of the three directions.

exact-dft.direct-pr-41: This proof reuses Jacob Sussman's recursion for the exact Fourier transform with a larger building block from the integer multiplication line of work, repeated many times. Lean files check the repeated block and the rate that it certifies: a saving of \(4719/1562500\), about 0.00302016. The author stated the smaller saving 0.0030103 on purpose. It is the base-10 logarithm of 2 divided by 100, rounded to five significant digits, and the author chose it because the number looks fun.
exact-dft.direct-pr-91: The new part is a different supplier of helper slots: a published word, a fixed sequence of 22,834 steps, that can only run forward. Sussman's certificate also needs a backward reading, so the proof builds the backward route from the forward route with a fixed wrapper of exchanges. Lean replays the word in seven segments and checks the rate \(727/232431\) for the 11340-fold tensor power.

3sum.direct-issue-35: The algorithm and its running-time accounting come from earlier entries by c0ldzy17 and Joshua Wharton. This version tunes the algorithm's parameters more finely so that its two largest cost terms nearly match, computes the logarithm bounds to more digits and tightens the safety margins. Lean checks that the resulting exponent holds.
3sum.direct-issue-92: The new part is a weighted downset cache, with costs 0, 512 and 1025. Lean checks the whole solver: its correctness, its resources and its running time, with exact logarithm certificates for the exponent.
3sum.direct-issue-99: The new part is the weighted cache: digit costs 0, 1369 and 2740, a new ternary profile and two new evaluation points. Lean checks the whole solver, its correctness and its running time. The submission also states, and proves in Lean outside our problem statement, that in its own cache model no choice of profile, costs, threshold and multipliers goes below 1.92027940818, so tuning it can lower the exponent by at most 0.000000000005 more. Our verifier checked only the running-time bound.

apsp.joshuaqfex-apsp-2026: The author found better tuning values for the all-pairs shortest paths construction. A Lean file checks 47 inequalities on those values and the exact identities between the stages of the construction.

subset-sum.yannouli-subset-sum-0-4876723-2026: The new part is a rule for where the certificates of filter 3 start and stop, plus new parameter margins. A written note proves the rule, and a script with exact fractions confirms the numbers.

integer-factoring.rudich-rousseau-2026: The machine finds the smallest prime factor one bit at a time: for each prefix, it counts the divisors of \(N\) that start with it. The count comes from a network that checks a Schönhage–Strassen multiplication, evaluated with the counting engine of Anthropic's 3-SAT preprint, proved again here. Lean proves the time bound for one machine and every \(k\). The paper's Conjecture 1, a faster rate, is only stated. It is not proved and scores nothing.
integer-factoring.1337isnot1337-half-2026: A Lean theorem proves that factoring \(b\)-bit numbers takes time \(2^{O(b/\sqrt{\log b})}\). Rudich and Rousseau only stated this rate as Conjecture 1. The proof combines Anthropic's clique evaluator (from its Exponential Time Hypothesis work) with their factoring reduction. Our verifier checked the proof with two independent kernels.

3sat.openai-eth-2026: The count of satisfying assignments is written as a sum over all assignments of products of clause values. Each variable in a clause is replaced by a linear form that depends on a parameter. At chosen nonzero values of the parameter, the variables split into groups that interact only through a few shared sums, so each group is counted on its own. The true count is then recovered by interpolation. The Lean proof gives a slightly weaker rate with the same score.
3sat.anthropic-eth-2026: The count is written as a sum over a graph. Its nodes are groups of clauses and its edges carry the shared bits. An identity for eight squares rewrites each costly pair of edges as a signed sum of terms that each cost fewer bits. Each level of the recursion merges the nodes into fewer groups and lowers the bits that cross between them. A sparsification step bounds the clauses by the variables. Lean checks the full time bound.

directed-sssp.directed-sssp-2026: Vals AI keeps the recursion of Ran Duan et al. (2025) and changes its local searches. A search counts a vertex whose distance does not improve as an unexplored leaf, and deletes for good each edge into a vertex whose distance is final, so its cost does not depend on vertex degrees. A larger search size saves work per vertex and adds work per edge. At \(m=n\log^{3/4}n\) the balance costs \(n\log^{11/12}n\), below \(n\log n\). Lean checks the distances the program outputs, and its running time.

integer-multiplication.text: Records from this repository build on OpenAI's multiplication method. An author changes the construction's parameters or interfaces and re-checks that the inequalities still hold, usually with Lean files. The bounds are conditional on OpenAI's reduction of fixed-tape multiplication and on the interfaces each submission cites. The repository's maintainer reviews a submission by merging it. We have not rerun the checks ourselves.
